anatomy.lede: A snowy owl is a heavy, round-headed owl wrapped in dense white feathers, with forward-facing yellow eyes and a neck that lets it scan the open tundra without moving its body.

hotspots.label: Head
hotspots.text: Like other owls it can swivel its head about 270 degrees, three-quarters of the way round, to scan for prey.

hotspots.label: Eye
hotspots.text: Bright yellow eyes face forwards. This owl hunts mostly in daylight, often watching from a post, rock or low rise.

hotspots.label: Bill
hotspots.text: The black, hooked bill is largely hidden in the feathers of the face.

hotspots.label: Dark barring
hotspots.text: White feathers are marked with dusky brown spots and bars. Females usually carry more markings, while some adults become almost pure white with age.

hotspots.label: Wing tips
hotspots.text: The ends of the flight feathers are very soft and feathery, which helps the owl fly almost silently.

senses.lede: On the treeless tundra, a snowy owl watches by day and listens for what it cannot see.

senses.name: Sight
senses.text: Unusually for an owl, it hunts mainly by day, scanning open ground from a perch before swooping on prey.

senses.name: Hearing
senses.text: Sharp hearing lets it pinpoint a vole moving beneath the snow, then pounce and grab it without ever seeing it.

body.lede: Living year-round where winters are long and dark, the snowy owl's body is built for cold.

systems.title: Feathers to the toes
systems.text: The feathers on its legs and feet are more densely layered than in owls of warmer climates, insulating the feet against snow and ice.

systems.title: Quiet wings
systems.text: Owl flight feathers have soft fringes and a velvety surface. A 2020 review suggests these mainly reduce the noise of feathers rubbing together as the wings move.

systems.title: A big appetite
systems.text: An owl needs several lemmings or voles a day just to survive, and a family with chicks can eat dozens a day.

genome.lede: A chromosome-level snowy owl genome, from a captive-bred female, was shared as a preprint in 2024 and published in 2026. It turned out to be one of the most repeat-rich bird genomes known.

findings.title: Unusually full of repeats
findings.text: About 28% of the snowy owl genome is repetitive DNA, compared with an average of around 10% in other birds — among the highest share reported for any bird.

findings.title: Giant centromere arrays
findings.text: Most of these repeats are satellite DNA at the centromeres, forming large blocks on several chromosomes — one of the biggest centromere expansions found in birds.

findings.title: New centromeres, new species?
findings.text: The owl's centromeres sit in different places from the chicken's, at points where chromosomes have been rearranged. The authors suggest this rapid change may have helped the snowy owl become a separate species.

mind.lede: Mostly solitary outside the breeding season, snowy owls communicate with displays and a surprising range of calls.

studies.title: Courtship displays
studies.text: Males court and threaten with displays both in the air and on the ground.

studies.title: Many voices
studies.text: Males hoot, mainly to defend territory. Both sexes also give barking 'rick, rick, rick' and 'kre kre kre' calls, mews and hisses, especially when disturbed near the nest.

studies.title: Sit and wait
studies.text: Snowy owls usually hunt from posts, rocks or the ground, watching quietly. They also snatch fish from the water's surface and even catch prey while walking.

survival.lede: Adults have few enemies, but eggs and chicks on an open tundra nest are exposed.

tactics.title: A guard on duty
tactics.text: While the female incubates and broods, the male stands guard near the nest.

tactics.title: Dive-bombs and decoys
tactics.text: Both parents dive at approaching predators and use distraction displays to lure them away from the nest.

threats.title: Collisions and shooting
threats.text: Common causes of death include collisions with vehicles, power lines and aircraft, shooting, electrocution and entanglement in fishing gear.

threats.title: A warming Arctic
threats.text: Climate change may be one of the biggest threats, as the Arctic is warming almost twice as fast as the global average.

life.lede: A snowy owl's breeding year depends on lemmings: in good years a pair raises a large brood, in poor years it may not breed at all.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: The female lays an egg about every two days; a clutch can reach 16 eggs when prey is extremely abundant.

stages.name: Nestling
stages.text: Chicks hatch roughly a day or two apart, so a brood ranges widely in size. They leave the nest on foot at 14–26 days, before they can fly.

stages.name: Fledgling
stages.text: Young owls master flight at about eight weeks old, and parents keep feeding them for several weeks until they can hunt.

stages.name: Adult
stages.text: Young owls are thought to be ready to breed at about two years old.

lifespan.value: Oldest known wild bird at least 9 years 5 months; 28 years in captivity
